intro: Free discussion guides for using Medics Musings episodes in residency didactics, medical school small groups, journal clubs, nursing education and grand rounds. Each guide pairs one short episode with learning objectives, discussion questions and a quick activity. Satire gets people talking about things they'd rather not.
note: These guides are not accredited for CME or CE credit. Programs are welcome to use them within their own accredited activities. Episodes are satirical and AI-generated; characters and “facts” in them may be fictional, which is part of what makes them good discussion starters.

guides.audience: Residents, fellows and students who present at conferences; chief residents and faculty who run them
objectives: Identify the unwritten rules of a department's teaching conference and who they serve.
Critique common presentation habits (slide overload, running long, dodging questions) using examples from the episode.
Draft a short set of presentation norms your program would actually endorse.
questions: Which of the “commandments” did you recognize from your own institution? Which ones made you uncomfortable because they're true?
Satire exaggerates real hierarchies. What does the episode suggest about who gets to ask questions at grand rounds, and who stays quiet?
What makes a grand rounds talk memorable? Think of the best and worst you've attended.
How has moving conferences online changed attendance, participation and learning?
If you could rewrite one commandment for the next generation of trainees, what would it say?
guides.activity: In pairs, write a “commandment” your program should keep and one it should retire. Share and vote.

guides.audience: Surgical residents and students; anyone teaching technology, simulation or professionalism
guides.theme: Technology, tactile skill and the surgeon–patient relationship
objectives: Describe “tissue sense” and how tactile feedback informs surgical judgment.
Compare what is gained and lost moving from open to laparoscopic to robotic surgery.
Discuss how trainees can build judgment when they rarely operate open.
questions: Dr. Gordon chose surgery to touch and cradle pathology in his hands. What drew you to your field, and has technology changed it?
How would you explain “tissue sense” to a first-year student? Can it be taught on a simulator or through a console?
What does a patient gain from minimally invasive and robotic surgery? What might they lose that they never see?
The essay describes surgery behind a glass partition. Where else in medicine has technology put distance between clinician and patient?
If the next generation of surgeons rarely operates open, what should residency programs do about it?
guides.activity: List three pieces of information you get from touch during an exam or operation. For each, name what replaces it when you can't touch, and what that replacement misses.

guides.audience: Geriatrics, internal medicine and family medicine trainees; nursing students; long-term care staff
guides.theme: Dignity, shame and technology in caring for older adults
objectives: Discuss how intimate care affects the dignity of older adults and their relationships with family and aides.
Evaluate potential benefits and harms of care robots in long-term care.
Identify the parts of care that technology should not replace.
questions: The narrator says shame doesn't transfer to a machine. Is that a good thing? When might it be a problem?
Gerald asks for consent before every step. How consistently do human caregivers do the same?
“A robot that replaces your Sunday visit is an abandonment with good UX.” Where is the line between support and replacement?
How should consent work for care technology when a resident has cognitive impairment?
What would you want a care robot to do for your own parent, and what would you never want it to do?
guides.activity: Rewrite the robot's consent script for a resident with moderate dementia. What changes?

guides.audience: Medical students on their first clinical rotations; neurology and ethics teaching
guides.theme: Hierarchy, informed consent and learning procedures on patients
objectives: Recognize how hierarchy can push trainees into procedures they don't understand.
Discuss informed consent and the patient's perspective when students perform procedures.
Explain the real purpose of caloric testing and why bedside tests carried more weight before modern imaging.
questions: The chief resident's instructions sound authoritative and are nonsense. How would a student in 1972 know? How would one know today?
What should the student have done when the plan didn't make sense? What makes speaking up hard?
What did the patient understand about what was about to happen to him? What would informed consent look like here?
Which procedures do students do on patients today, and how is consent obtained for their involvement?
What “ice water calorics” of today, confidently taught practices, might look absurd in fifty years?
guides.activity: Role-play the moment the student is handed the bucket. One person is the student, one the resident. Practice a respectful way to ask for clarification or decline.

guides.audience: Psychiatry residents, psychology trainees, social work and counseling students
objectives: Define transference and countertransference.
Identify transference cues in a session.
Discuss how and when a therapist might name transference with a client.
questions: What cues in the session signaled that the client was relating to the therapist the way she related to a parent?
How did the therapist respond? What might she have been feeling (countertransference)?
The sportscast format treats insight as a game-winning play. What does that get right, and wrong, about how change happens in therapy?
How do transference reactions show up in non-psychiatric settings, such as a surgeon's clinic or an emergency department?
How do you tell the difference between transference and a reasonable reaction to something the therapist actually did?
guides.activity: Commentate a short (fictional) session transcript in pairs: one person calls the “plays” while the other explains the psychology.

guides.audience: Residents, faculty and wellness committees; any interprofessional group
guides.theme: Burnout, humor and coping in medicine
objectives: Describe the dimensions of burnout and its main system-level drivers.
Discuss the role and the limits of humor as a coping strategy.
Identify one system change and one peer-support practice your group could adopt.
questions: The story is fictional. Why does the idea of Freud prescribing stand-up comedy land with clinicians?
When does humor in medicine help, and when does it become gallows humor that harms patients or colleagues?
What causes burnout in your setting? How much is individual, and how much is the system?
Wellness programs are sometimes criticized for asking individuals to fix system problems. Is that fair here?
Who do you talk to after a hard day? What would make that easier?
guides.activity: Each person writes one true, funny, patient-safe story from work on a card. Read a few aloud. Then discuss what the stories reveal about the stresses of the job.

guides.audience: Surgical residents and OR teams (surgeons, nurses, anesthesia, radiology technologists)
guides.theme: Operating room systems, delays and teamwork
objectives: Identify common causes of operating room delays and equipment failures.
Discuss how teams can address recurring OR frustrations without blame.
Relate the basic mechanics of laparoscopic surgery to its practical challenges.
questions: Which of the ten “laws of physics” describe real problems in your OR? Which ones have you personally witnessed?
The radiology technologist's location “is indeterminate.” How does the humor land for different members of the team?
Pick one recurring delay. What system change, not a person trying harder, would fix it?
How do surgeons compensate for the fulcrum effect and loss of touch in laparoscopy?
How can satire help, or hurt, conversations about OR culture?
guides.activity: Write an eleventh law of physics for your own OR, then turn it into a quality-improvement aim statement.

guides.audience: Internal medicine, geriatrics and family medicine trainees; medical students
guides.theme: Longitudinal care, the older patient's story and diagnostic uncertainty
objectives: Discuss how a long doctor–patient relationship shapes diagnosis and care.
Practice interpreting physical findings in the hands and nails of an older patient.
Reflect on how the electronic record and problem lists represent, and miss, a patient's life.
questions: The narrator has cared for Sylvia for over twenty years. What does he notice that a new clinician would miss?
What can the hands and nails tell you on exam? Which findings in the story are real signs, and which are satire?
Sylvia's problem list is “as long as the Bronx telephone directory,” yet no one knows her story. What belongs in a record that doesn't fit in a problem list?
How do you balance curiosity about a patient's past with respect for what they choose not to share?
What happens to patients like Sylvia when their long-time physician retires?
guides.activity: Write a two-sentence “who this person is” summary for a patient you know well, the kind that never makes it into the problem list.
